Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-23
Start time (UTC): 15:00
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Ruiz (Redwood SE), Nina Patel (Redwood Solutions), Lena Park (Peregrine ML), Tom Baxter (Peregrine Platform), Arun Singh (CTO), Priya Rao (SRE)

Auto Summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete):
- Deep dive on JSON/structured-output mode overheads and constrained decoding performance.
- Discussed KV cache hit patterns, batching strategies, and quantization tradeoffs for on-prem/VPC deployments.
- Agreed next steps: Redwood to share microbenchmarks and KV toggles; Peregrine to share traffic traces; schedule PoC kickoff.

Topics:
- JSON mode vs free-text parsing overhead
- Constrained decoding/token filtering costs
- KV cache priming and eviction effects on latency
- Batching windows and tail-latency tradeoffs
- Quantization profiles impact on throughput and determinism
- VPC/on-prem I/O and kernel selection differences

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: okay hi everyone, thanks for carving time, I'll kick off, this is Maya from Redwood, alongside Carlos and Nina, um we're here to run through the constrained-decode and JSON mode perf stuff you flagged.
[00:12] Arun Singh: thanks Maya, yes we're mainly worried about structured output correctness and the latency hit we've been seeing when we force JSON-mode.  Our dashboards show 30 to 50% slower p95s on JSON mode compared to free-form text.
[00:25] Carlos Ruiz: yeah, that matches what we've seen in a couple of accounts. The overhead is usually a mix of token-level constraints, the extra decoding checks, plus any post-parse reparsing when the model drifts. We'll try to unpack those today.
[00:39] Tom Baxter: quick context, our typical request is a 3-turn convo plus a 1k token max response, majority of requests are short ~120 tokens. We also have a KV-backed store for user profiles that we expect the model to consult 60% of the time.
[00:55] Lena Park: and we run on a private VPC with per-tenant volumes, so on-prem-ish I/O is a factor; we also plan to try a 4-bit quantized variant to save cost.
[01:10] Maya Chen: great, that helps. Carlos, do you want to show the benchmark slide? (small rustle)
[01:15] Carlos Ruiz: sure, let me share screen—okay, um, the raw numbers: baseline free-text on a standard A100-like node with our runtime gave ~28 ms/token throughput at 8k context, JSON-mode with strict parse and constrained decoding jumps to ~38 ms/token in our test, so ~35% penalty. But that number varies with sequence length distribution and how often the parser rejects partial outputs, causing extra rollback tokens.
[01:45] Priya Rao: rollback tokens? can you expand, sorry I'm catching up.
[01:48] Carlos Ruiz: yeah so if you enforce strict JSON closing braces and the model emits something invalid mid-stream, our constrained-decoding path can either backtrack a few tokens or apply higher beam constraints which increases compute per token. The worst case is when the generator loops and you end up with repeated retries.
[02:05] Arun Singh: hmm, in our logs we see about 3% of responses retried. Could be that.
[02:10] Maya Chen: also worth noting our runtime does KV cache integration at generation time—if the model asks for a retrieved slot, we stitch in the KV result and that can change token probabilities, sometimes triggering invalid sequences if prompts use brittle templates.
[02:24] Tom Baxter: so is KV cache hit causing more invalid JSONs?
[02:28] Carlos Ruiz: occasionally—especially when the KV content includes unescaped characters, or long user free text that breaks the template. We have heuristics to sanitize but depending on your sanitize profile it can alter fluency.
[02:40] Lena Park: we do store raw user comments in KV, lots of punctuation. We can pre-escape, but that will bloat token counts.
[02:48] Maya Chen: right, tradeoff: escaping increases token length, escaping reduces parse failures. For strict-mode we recommend lighter KV trimming plus a deterministic templating layer in the prompt.
[02:57] Carlos Ruiz: another angle is batching. If you use larger batching windows to improve throughput, your contention on KV lookups may increase p99 tail because of synchronous lookups. Redwood supports async prefetch for KV but it's dependent on your deployment topology.
[03:15] Priya Rao: can you explain async prefetch? We run in VPC with private backbone storage.
[03:19] Carlos Ruiz: async prefetch means the serving runtime issues KV retrievals ahead of the decode step based on predicted keys; we cache them in-memory (KV cache) to avoid blocking the decode thread. In VPC/on-prem setups, network variance makes prefetching riskier, but it's still net-win if your access patterns are stable.
[03:36] Arun Singh: latency numbers for prefetch vs sync?
[03:40] Carlos Ruiz: sync lookup on our bench (local NVMe adjacent) is ~3-6 ms per lookup; over VPC with 2-3 hop NAT + firewall it can go to 15-30 ms. Prefetch amortizes that across batch and reduces p95s.
[03:55] Tom Baxter: hmm that maps to our spike windows. What about quantization? If we go 4-bit, do we risk more parse failures?
[04:02] Carlos Ruiz: quantization mostly affects logits fidelity; in practice deterministic structured output can degrade slightly with aggressive quant like 3/4-bit, especially on edge cases causing off-by-a-token errors. We recommend validating with your eval prompts. Our Find/Recommend suggestion: run A/B on a small sample with and without strict JSON and measure "valid JSON" rate.
[04:22] Lena Park: we can do that. How big of a sample?
[04:25] Carlos Ruiz: 10k queries across your 72-hour traffic is usually enough to get stable estimates. Also add the failure cases to an eval set for continuous monitoring.
[04:36] Maya Chen: quick interjection—there's also runtime-level mitigations: deterministic token filters, constrained decoding with prefix enforcement, and a low-cost reparsing stage where we run a fast structured-validator and only re-decode when required. The reparsing path is cheaper than full re-decode in many cases.
[04:53] Arun Singh: what's "fast structured-validator"?
[04:55] Carlos Ruiz: it's a streaming JSON validator that runs as tokens come out; it's O(n) linear and only flags errors when braces or quotes are mismatched. If it's a small mismatch we can attempt a local token-level correction.
[05:08] Tom Baxter: does that add latency?
[05:10] Carlos Ruiz: marginal CPU time, usually <1 ms per response for short outputs, but in pathological cases it triggers re-decode which is the costly part.
[05:18] Priya Rao: what about your reported 35% token-level penalty earlier—how much of that is validation vs constrained-decode checks?
[05:24] Carlos Ruiz: rough split: ~60% decoding checks/backtrack when strict enforcement is enabled, ~25% additional parse/validation cost, ~15% overhead from longer tokenized inputs due to escaping. But numbers will change if your retry rate is high.
[05:38] Maya Chen: also note hardware kernel differences. On some on-prem GPUs with older cuDNN or different tensor cores, quant 4-bit kernels may be less optimized, so throughput drops further. That's why we do kernel selection and runtime compilation per host.
[05:52] Lena Park: we run mixed fleet: two host types, older 8xx gen and newer 10xx gen. Is that a problem?
[05:57] Carlos Ruiz: mixed fleets complicate p95 SLAs. Smart routing helps: route strict-json low-latency traffic to the newer hosts and route cheaper batches to older ones. That said if you want total isolation, Dedicated pools are better; for on-prem we can pin model variants.
[06:12] Arun Singh: you mentioned routing—does Redwood support auto-fallback to a lighter model when p99 spikes?
[06:17] Maya Chen: yes, policy-based routing and automatic fallback to a compatible, lower-cost model is supported. You can define SLOs that if latency or error rate crosses threshold we route to a dequantized or smaller model.
[06:27] Tom Baxter: curious about cost comparison for JSON mode: any rule of thumb?
[06:31] Carlos Ruiz: rule of thumb: expect 20-50% token-cost increase when enforcing strict structured outputs depending on failure/retry rates. Batching can reduce per-token compute but increases tail latencies. So you trade tokens vs latency.
[06:45] Maya Chen: real-world example: a fintech customer moved to a two-stage approach—first a compact model to draft JSON, then a higher-capacity model to validate and fill missing fields. That reduced overall cost by ~18% while keeping validity high.
[06:58] Lena Park: two-stage sounds interesting. Any caveats?
[07:01] Carlos Ruiz: complexity increases; you need orchestration and latency budget split. But we have built-in support for multi-stage pipelines and can route outputs between them.
[07:11] Priya Rao: on the VPC side, what about KMS latency when decrypting prompts or user keys? We saw a spike once when KMS was throttled.
[07:19] Maya Chen: KMS calls should be cached and not in the hot path; we advise using short-lived decrypted envelopes and local HSM integration for on-prem when latency is critical. We also recommend reactive cache warming during peak windows.
[07:33] Tom Baxter: practical question—what should we test in the PoC to validate JSON-mode viability?
[07:37] Carlos Ruiz: test matrix suggestion in order: (1) 10k sample with strict JSON mode on current model, measure valid rate and retry rate; (2) same sample with lightweight pre-escape of KV content; (3) run 4-bit quant variant on same sample; (4) test batching at your target QPS with async prefetch enabled/disabled; (5) run on your VPC topology to measure lookup latencies. We'll provide scripts for each.
[08:00] Maya Chen: we'll attach the scripts and a perf spreadsheet. We'll also include curl examples to flip KV cache on/off.
[08:07] Arun Singh: do you have a recommended batch size / window for 120-token typical responses?
[08:11] Carlos Ruiz: for mostly short responses we see best latency with micro-batching 8-16 and a 10-30 ms aggregation window. If you need lower p95, go smaller; if you want cheaper p50, go larger.
[08:23] Lena Park: ok that fits our SLO of 200 ms p95.
[08:27] Priya Rao: about the sanitizer you mentioned—what's the recommended approach for KV contents?
[08:31] Carlos Ruiz: strip control chars, normalize whitespace, optionally hash very long free-form fields and pass a summary placeholder into KV. We can add a lightweight sanitize library to your pipeline.
[08:42] Tom Baxter: are there any Redwood-specific SDK flags we should be aware of to minimize invalid JSONs?
[08:45] Maya Chen: yes—use the structured_output mode with "graceful_fallback": true, and enable "early_validator" and "kv_prefetch": true for VPC. Carlos will send the exact SDK flags.
[08:57] Carlos Ruiz: also set "max_retry_attempts" to 2 and "retry_strategy": "repair_then_decode" to avoid long loops.
[09:05] Arun Singh: nice. Let's talk about monitoring—how do we track structured-output regressions in prod?
[09:10] Maya Chen: Redwood Console supports per-route validity metrics, e.g., JSON_VALID_RATE, PARSE_RETRY_RATE, and token-level deltas. You can set alerts on parse regression and auto-roll back deployment if validity drops.
[09:23] Lena Park: can we store the invalid examples for audit? We have privacy concerns but want to keep anonymized samples.
[09:29] Maya Chen: yes, Redwood supports storing hashed/anonymized snippets, and you can configure retention. For Private deployments you can keep everything in your tenant storage.
[09:38] Carlos Ruiz: quick note about determinism: if your application requires byte-exact JSON every time, constrained decoding plus temperature=0 and forced tokens is the way. But that increases retries if model isn't trained for that template, so consider a tiny fine-tune or instruction-tuning with your template.
[09:58] Tom Baxter: we don't want to fine-tune initially. Is there a middle path?
[10:02] Carlos Ruiz: yes—prompt engineering: few-shot examples, structured instruction, and token biasing toward expected keys helps a lot. Also a light post-filter that fills missing keys with defaults can reduce visible failures.
[10:15] Maya Chen: wrapping up recommendations for the PoC: start small, measure JSON_VALID_RATE, iterate on sanitizer and batching, try 4-bit on a holdout, and test prefetch in VPC. We'll send the scripts and sample configs.
[10:28] Arun Singh: sounds good. Any blockers on your side for the PoC?
[10:31] Maya Chen: none, we'll need an access account for the test cluster and your 72-hour trace. We'll provide infra checklist.
[10:38] Priya Rao: timeline? We prefer kickoff early June.
[10:41] Maya Chen: we'll target week of 2025-06-09 for PoC kickoff after you share traces.
[10:45] Carlos Ruiz: I'll include the constrained-decode microbenchmarks and kernel notes; watch out for mixed fleet kernel gaps.
[10:52] Tom Baxter: very helpful, thank you.
[10:55] Maya Chen: thanks everyone. Quick recap of action items (auto): Maya to send perf sheet and configs, Carlos to share scripts, Lena to export request distribution. We'll follow up in email and schedule the PoC kickoff.
[11:08] Arun Singh: thanks all, bye.
